title: The pursuit of beauty is fragmenting the self
subtitle: The philosophy behind social media and the beauty industry
author: Ellen Atlanta
body:
Social media platforms don’t just change how we look, they change what a self is for. Author of Pixel Flesh,Ellen Atlanta, argues beauty culture intensifies and extends until our bodies fragment. Perfected images used to appear only occasionally, on Hollywood screens or in glossy magazines. Now Kylie Jenner inhabits the same screen as your cousin and the friend from school who became an influencer. The worry isn’t that beauty or vanity exists; it’s that our digitized beauty culture has weaponized them against the self.

In 1972, Susan Sontag wrote: “Men present themselves as face-and-body, a physical whole. Women are split, as men are not, into a body and a face—each judged by somewhat different standards.” Now, in the age of platform capitalism, it is so much worse than that.

Platforms don’t just change how we look; they change what a self is for. In the economy of the industrialized digital gaze, people become sets of parts to be remodelled. Crops, lenses, editing apps and tweakments train us into part-thinking: lips, waist, chin, nose, gonial jaw angle, nasolabial folds. Beauty culture intensifies and extends until our bodies fragment.

The self becomes an asset to be tuned, tracked and improved before visibility is permitted.
Philosophers have warned against treating persons merely as means. But platforms that reward superficiality invite exactly that: we instrumentalize ourselves. Phenomenologists demarcate the lived body (the one I am) from the object body (the one I look at): filters and editing tools coach us towards the latter, to regard ourselves as voyeurs. Value theory distinguishes intrinsic from instrumental worth; metrics in our hyper-visual digital realm tilt us toward measuring being by performing. And if flourishing is the aim of life, eudaimonia can hardly survive when the telos is perpetual re-optimisation—there is no arrival, only the next fix. Makeover is a present tense verb because it was never about the finished product; the goal, in this market, is endless reconstruction.

The worry isn’t that beauty or vanity exists; it’s that our digitized beauty culture has weaponized them against the self.

Beauty culture intensifies and extends until our bodies fragment.

Not long ago, perfected images appeared only occasionally—a billboard on your drive home, a glossy magazine spread, a movie. Hollywood once occupied a separate universe, and the boundary between aspiration and actuality was less ambiguous. Now, Kylie Jenner inhabits the same screen as your cousin and the friend from school who became an influencer. Context collapses. The airbrushed and edited face is no longer a separate standard, but an ideal that has infiltrated your inner circle, one you could see hundreds of times an hour—not just on celebrities, but on the faces of people you know and love.

What’s more, in a world of thumbnails, profile photos and maximising visibility on a grid, fragmented faces and bodies are the focal point. We curate dismantled images of ourselves, posting just a pair of lips, collarbones, breasts, a ribcage, or a bum. This is how social media fragmentated the self into parts to be perfected and maintained. By fragmenting, we intensify the beauty standard applied to each part, creating a disembodied blueprint for how we “should” look. Beauty becomes a jigsaw puzzle of perfect pieces, each appraised in isolation, but required to fit together in a perfect composite. Social media delivers a feed of dismembered women.

AI filters and precision editing make perfection an ongoing simulation. We live inside an experimental loop where every photo is a hypothesis: if I carve the jaw, whiten the teeth, pinch the waist, inflate the lips, slim the nose and smooth the hips, does the number of likes go up? Feedback arrives instantaneously as likes, comments and shares. We are refined, over and over again, to perform as better objects.

SUGGESTED VIEWING The ugly truth behind beauty With Jessica DeFino

The consequences are everywhere. Girls as young as ten talk about their “pores”, needing to always look “perfect” and “filtered”; while half of secondary-school girls are considering some form of surgical intervention. Research by Dove in 2021 found 80 percent of girls editing their appearance by age thirteen, and 77 percent aged ten to seventeen trying to hide or change at least one body part before posting. During research for Pixel Flesh, I met fourteen-year-olds who refuse to leave the house for fear of looking “too ugly” for real life; online, they perfect their self-presentation.

There is nothing wrong in looking after our teeth for hygiene purposes; fixing a deviated septum to breathe better; or expressing ourselves with make-up. The problem isn’t modification itself. But fragmentation turns once-occasional interventions into a never-ending spiral, because a part can always be improved, and the self can always be further split. The standard accelerates and accumulates: not a single surgery, but one after another. We may start with orthodontics for those with unaligned teeth, or a careful clean for those with cavities. Then braces become the standard for all, no matter your smile. Then not just braces but teeth whitening; no more natural teeth but veneers; not just veneers, but an entire set of healthy teeth filed down to points on the black market and re-coded to fit the image of what a “normal” mouth should be. Then the beauty market moves to the next hyperfixation, and we fragment ourselves into ever smaller parts. For all this, we are no healthier or happier, and our fragments litter the timeline—a body sold for parts.

Social media delivers a feed of dismembered women.

In our increasingly online lives, it becomes more important to be seen living a beautiful life than actually living one. When the money that might have built skills or security is reallocated to upkeep; when adolescent years meant to be spent experimenting and pushing boundaries are occupied by endless optimization; when the anxiety of being seen unedited keeps girls from school trips, sports, job interviews, or simply going outside, the problem is not merely aesthetic: it degrades personhood and recodes the physical self as an unceasing project that is defective by default.

The harms work at the level of personhood and participation in public life. Self-objectification is a form of dissociation: the subject evacuates the body to scrutinize it. Over time, the inner narrator talks exclusively in images. Your value is not “I am” but “I look.” Activities that were once agentic—running for the train, dancing at a party, raising your hand in class—are interrupted by self-surveillance. Did my arm wobble on video? Does my skin look bad in this light? When you relate to your body as a display item, sensation flattens and spontaneity withers. In phenomenological terms, you stop being a body and start having one, a lump of matter you micromanage from the outside. It is an anaesthetic disguised as aesthetic.

The social consequences are unevenly distributed. The beauty tax, as it stands, falls heavier on women and girls in terms of money spent, but also, more critically, in hours passed. The promise that “anyone can be famous now” morphs into a funnel: more girls calculate that the efficient route to status or security is audience-first. Meanwhile, in schools and workplaces, norms harden. If a third of your peers are smoothing, brightening and contouring before they post, it becomes more difficult to show up with a human face. The burden shifts from preference to requirement.

A profile picture study found that girls choose tight crops—face or upper torso—whereas boys more often choose full-body images, even at thumbnail size. The close crop invites judgment of parts; the distant shot says take me or leave me. It’s a small datum with a large question hidden inside: who gets to be whole?

But the impact is not confined to girls. Boys are increasingly being pulled in through a different doorway as fragmentation fortifies its grip. From gym culture’s hypertrophied numbers to facial masculinity hacks with their pseudo-anthropometric jargon—canthal tilt, mewing, maxilla—and increasing steroid use, the same logic applies: quantify, isolate, improve the part. The price is the same fracturing of the body: from agent to asset.
Many of us know the fun of self-expression, of beauty culture, of being made new—that make-up can be play, that there is a thrill, and even a sense of peace, in seeing your inner vision made visible. Joy isn’t the enemy. The difference is compulsion. When the feed adjudicates your worth, performance becomes compulsory, and what was once expression becomes a mask welded on.

SUGGESTED READING Truth is dead, and that's a good thing By Steve Fuller

I argue that joyful adornment feels like a coalescence—the inner and outer elements of our truest selves playing together, the lived body animating the aesthetic. Pathological fragmentation and optimisation on the other hand, feels like a rupture—the inner self is held hostage by the outer’s demands, creating a wall between desire and actuality. One enlarges the person; the other hands the self over to society, diminishing as a result.
It matters that this is happening to children, because children have neither the understanding nor the psychological tools to refuse the game. A ten-year-old girl learning to regard her face as a fixable object loses her agency: an algorithm tells her who she is before she gets to decide. When a thirteen-year-old avoids the dentist because she can’t bear the thought of her teeth under bright lights, beauty culture threatens health. A body that must be prepared before it can be lived in will eventually be a body you detach from, and degrade.

None of this means we must abandon aesthetics or retreat from images. It does mean we need to redraw the moral perimeter. First, the obvious: we can build and demand different defaults. Whole-frame posting as a norm; no image edits as standard. Wellbeing nudges that interrupt the impulse to filter—“Why not post as is?”—are not nannying if they restore agency. Influencer pledges to disclose edits and procedures won’t cure the incentive problem, but they do make the game visible and encourage critical thought. Schools can teach gaze literacy alongside media literacy: not just how images are made, but how seeing trains being. The aim is not total abstinence but increased awareness; noticing the “choices” we make on autopilot; the parts of ourselves we slice, split and serve on social media without a second thought.

The language we use about ourselves can change too. Ask any woman or girl and she will effortlessly produce a list of her own body parts that are defective. She may tell you that some parts of herself are “okay” and perhaps name some that she likes, but rarely. When asked to describe their bodies, women reduce themselves to components. Men, on the other hand, view their bodies as single units. The men asked to describe their body in a University of Sussex study tended to describe what it could do. The women in the study, however, valued their body more as decorative objects, based only on aesthetic value. The fragmentation extended past their physical selves and into their sentient selves—a fracture between the body and its entitlement to value purely for being. We can recalibrate our attention away from aesthetics and towards action and agency—instead of thinking “my arms need to be thinner” we can redirect our thoughts to “my arms allow me to…”—reintroducing capability as a site of pride, as a counterweight to the object gaze.

In our increasingly online lives, it becomes more important to be seen living a beautiful life than actually living one.

Thirdly, we should be conscious of the commercial structure. A surgical-industrial complex now medicalises normal variation in bodies and faces, and the path from care to correction is paved with profit. Procedures that once restored function now promise conformity. As a result, many women pursue cosmetic surgery now not to become “beautiful” but to appear “normal,” a fact surely more terrifying. Normality has been moved as we increasingly fragment and perfect, and each move is billable. When trend cycles enter flesh—hip dips out, jawlines in, labia minora out, chin balancing in—we are no longer shopping for clothes but for features. Fast fashion logic becomes fast body logic. You were never meant to feel finished.

Finally, there is the matter of mercy. We are all implicated; we all look, we all appear, we all judge, we all desire. The fragmentation doesn’t only split us from ourselves; it sets us against one another. I have known the flicker of envy comparing parts of myself to another, and the mean relief when her perfection cracks and she joins the rest of us in the broken girls’ club. We don’t heal fragmentation by inventing a new target for the gaze. We heal by calling each other back into wholeness, by refusing to play the game of parts. 
The task is not to reject beauty or social media platforms, but to refuse the redesign of self into a project forever incomplete. The goal is to live as a body; to pick up the pieces and endeavor to make ourselves whole again.
